issues.legal_issue: A compensation award should remain undisturbed where the higher court has increased it and the claimant has not shown that the land was undervalued.
material_facts: For a smaller parcel, the trial court awarded compensation and the High Court increased that award.
The claimant did not show that the High Court had undervalued the land.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s compensation award for the smaller parcel remains undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no good reason to interfere with the High Court’s award because the claimant had not shown that the land was undervalued.

rule.if: appeal_from_land_compensation_award and higher_court_increased_compensation and not undervaluation_shown

predicates.appeal_from_land_compensation_award: A claimant appealed the determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.higher_court_increased_compensation: The higher court increased the compensation awarded for the land.
predicates.undervaluation_shown: The claimant showed that the higher court had undervalued the land.

issues.definition: When a claimant appeals a land-compensation award, the higher court has increased compensation, and no undervaluation is shown, the higher court’s award remains undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A delay before development reaches acquired land may justify valuing it at a lower rate and deducting land set aside for roads and open spaces, but does not justify an additional present-value deduction for delayed payment.
material_facts: The larger parcels were situated in the interior, and the High Court considered that development would take about twelve years to reach them.
The High Court valued the land at a lower rate and deducted 25 percent for land required for roads and open spaces.
The High Court also made a further deduction using Miram’s Tables on the basis that the compensation would be received after the development delay.
In the companion case, the Court had upheld the lower valuation and the deduction for roads and open spaces, but rejected the further deduction for delayed payment.
issues.conclusion: The valuation and deduction for land required for roads and open spaces were upheld, but the further present-value deduction was set aside; compensation was to be calculated without that additional deduction.
issues.legal_principle: Applying its reasoning in Chimanlal Hargovinddas v. The Special Land Acquisition Officer, Poona, the Court held that the development delay could be reflected in the land valuation and that land needed for roads and open spaces could be deducted, but the amount of compensation should not be further reduced to derive a present value based on delayed receipt.

rule.if: appeal_from_land_compensation_award and land_is_interior and development_will_reach_land_later and land_must_be_set_aside_for_access_or_open_space

predicates.appeal_from_land_compensation_award: A claimant appealed the determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_is_interior: The acquired land is situated in the interior rather than in an area already reached by development.
predicates.development_will_reach_land_later: Development is expected to reach the acquired land only after a delay.
predicates.land_must_be_set_aside_for_access_or_ope: A portion of the land must be set aside for roads, open spaces, or similar development needs.

issues.definition: For an appeal concerning interior land that development will reach later and that requires land to be set aside for access or open space, compensation uses a lower land value and the land-use deduction without an additional deduction for delayed receipt.

issues.legal_issue: The entitlement of pending land-compensation appeals to enhanced solatium and interest depends on the Constitution Bench’s determination of the retrospective operation of the amending legislation.
material_facts: The appeals were pending before the Supreme Court on the date relevant to the statutory amendment.

The amendment provided for enhanced solatium and interest, and the Court treated entitlement under its transitional provision as dependent on whether the amendment applied to orders under appeal concerning earlier awards.
A Constitution Bench was expected to decide between the view in Bhag Singh and the view in Kamalajammanniavaru.
issues.conclusion: The appellants would receive the enhanced benefits if the Constitution Bench upheld the view in Bhag Singh and overruled the view in Kamalajammanniavaru; they would not receive those benefits if it affirmed the latter view.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 30(2) of the Central Amending Act, 1984, entitlement to the enhanced benefits under amended Sections 23(2) and 28 depended on the amendment’s retrospective operation. The Court left that question to the expected Constitution Bench decision on the differing views in Bhag Singh and Kamalajammanniavaru.

predicates.pending_land_compensation_appeal: A landowner has an appeal pending concerning an award of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.appeal_pending_on_relevant_cutoff: The appeal was pending on the date relevant to the transitional operation of the amendment.
predicates.constitution_bench_accepts_retroactive_a: The Constitution Bench adopts the view that the amendment applies retrospectively to qualifying orders under appeal.

issues.definition: A pending land-compensation appeal qualifies for enhanced benefits when it was pending on the relevant cutoff and the Constitution Bench accepts retrospective application; otherwise, those benefits do not apply under the Court’s stated condition.
